docs/1.overview.md.skeleton: Nuxt CLI
The Nuxt CLI runs, builds and inspects your Nuxt application from the command line.
Source

{0} is the {1} command: it runs the dev server, builds your application for production, scaffolds files, manages modules and answers questions about your project. It is a dependency of {2}, so a Nuxt project already has it.
Terminal

The binary is installed as {0}, and also as {1}, {2} and {3} for compatibility with older setups. Scaffolding a new project is a separate package, {4}, so that it can be run without a project to install into.
{0} is a third package: a standalone CLI with no dependencies, for running commands outside a project or installing globally.
Requirements
The CLI runs on Node v22.21+, v24.11+ or v26+, and imports TypeScript configuration natively on those versions. Nuxt 2 and {0} are not supported.
Running commands
Inside a project, your package manager runs the version the project depends on:
Terminal

Outside a project, or installed globally, {0} runs the same commands. It hands each one over to the {1} installed in the project when there is one, so the code that runs matches the version of Nuxt it sits alongside rather than whatever is on your machine. It falls back to its own bundled commands when there is no project CLI, when the project's copy predates v3.26, or when the project's copy does not know the command, so a project pinned to an older release still gets newer commands.
Global options
{0} may be passed before the command name as well as after it, which is useful in a monorepo:
Terminal
Commands that take a {0} positional treat an explicit {1} as an override of it. {2} on any command prints its arguments and options, and {3} prints the CLI version.
Mistyped commands and flags

An unrecognised command is matched against the ones that exist, and an unrecognised flag against the ones the command declares. In an interactive terminal you are offered the correction to run instead; otherwise it is reported as a warning, so a misspelled flag no longer looks like a flag that simply had no effect.
Project commands
A command the CLI does not provide is looked up as a {0} binary in your project, so a dependency can add a command of its own. This is how {1} works: it runs the {2} binary that {3} installs.
Shell completions
{0} prints a completion script, powered by {1}. It completes commands, flags and some flag values: ports and hosts for {2}, Nitro presets for {3}, and log levels.
{0} is also supported, and {1} has its own script which completes starter template names.
Completions work through your package manager too ({0}), if you install {1}tab's package manager completions{/1}.
Update notifications

Once a day the CLI checks in the background whether a newer Nuxt release exists and, if so, prints a short nudge to run {0} once the command has finished. The {1} dist-tag is read from the registry configured in your {2} and cached in your user-level {3}.

The nudge is not shown for prereleases, and not for a patch release within the same minor unless you are at least five patches behind. The check is skipped in CI, on StackBlitz, and when the output is not a terminal.
Set {0} or {1} to skip it for one run, or add {2} to your user-level {3} to opt out for good.
Networks and proxies

Commands that reach the network (installing a module, searching modules, downloading a template, checking for updates) report why a request failed rather than the raw error, and suggest the retry that is likely to work. Behind a proxy that re-signs TLS traffic that means {0}, pointing at your organisation's root certificate.

Node only reads proxy environment variables when {0} is set, and the CLI passes that setting on to the processes it spawns, so a package manager install started by {1} sees the same proxy configuration you do.
Prereleases
Every commit on {0} is published to the nightly channel:
Terminal
{0} scaffolds with it, and {1} scaffolds a project against the Nuxt nightly channel.
Builds for an individual pull request are published by {0}pkg.pr.new{/0} and linked from the pull request itself, which is the quickest way to check whether a fix works before it is released.
